title: Ice & Frozen Play
strapline: Cold in your hands, changing before your eyes.
intent: Ice is a real scientific material: it melts, cracks, floats and refreezes, and children can genuinely investigate it.
The shock of cold and the slow melt are absorbing sensory experiences that hold children's attention for a long time.
Freeing objects and animals frozen in ice gives play a real, motivating problem to solve.
It's rich in change-and-comparison talk — freezing, melting, harder, faster, slippery, drip.
Melting experiments build early cause-and-effect and prediction in the most hands-on way.
implementation: Freeze water in different containers, some with objects, animals or coloured water inside.
Offer warm water, salt, droppers, spoons and brushes so children can act on the ice and change it.
Sit alongside and wonder: 'The ice is melting — where is the water going? How could we make it faster?'
Set a real challenge: 'The little animal is frozen in — how can we rescue it?'
Name and compare the changes: 'This one melted quicker — why do you think that is?'
Feed in vocabulary — freeze, melt, solid, liquid, slippery — as children explore.
Keep warm water and towels close so cold hands don't end the play too soon.
key_questions: What is happening to the ice — and where is the water coming from?
How could we melt it more quickly to rescue what's inside?
Which melted faster — the one in warm water or in salt? Why?
How does the ice feel, and how does it change as you hold it?
What do you think will happen if we put it back in the freezer?

impact.text: Children explore the ice deeply — holding, pushing, watching — testing what it does.
Children notice, describe and predict the melting and freezing, and offer their own reasons.
Children try out ways to melt the ice faster — warm water, salt, rubbing — and compare what works.
Children persist with the rescue challenge, staying with a slow problem until the object is free.
Children use change-and-comparison vocabulary — melt, freeze, faster, slippery — accurately.
Children pour, scoop, drip and brush with growing fine-motor control.

enhancements: Objects, animals or 'treasure' frozen inside blocks of ice to rescue.
Warm water, salt, pipettes, spoons and small brushes for melting.
Coloured ice cubes to melt and mix on white trays.
A freezer challenge: freeze different things overnight and compare in the morning.
Magnifiers to watch cracks and drips up close.
A frosty-day walk to notice real ice, frost and puddles outdoors.

playing_exploring: Children investigate a genuinely changing material with all their senses.
They test everything they can do to the ice — push, warm, salt, rub.
active_learning: Children stay with the slow melt and the rescue, persisting until the object is freed.
creating_thinking: Children predict and explain what the ice will do, and compare which method melts it fastest.
